claim: PopuCATH is a novel naturally occurring cathelicidin identified from tree frog (Polypedates puerensis).
source: Herein, a novel naturally occurring cathelicidin (PopuCATH) from tree frog (Polypedates puerensis) did not show any direct anti-bacterial activity in vitro.
evidence: The manuscript describes the identification and characterization of PopuCATH from P. puerensis through peptide isolation and cDNA cloning.

claim: PopuCATH did not show any direct anti-bacterial activity in vitro.

claim: Intraperitoneal injection of PopuCATH before bacterial inoculation significantly reduced the bacterial load in tree frogs.

claim: The precursor of PopuCATH is composed of 179 amino acid residues.
source: The coding sequence of the precursor included 659 nucleotides that encodes a precursor containing 179 amino acid residues (Figure 1).

claim: PopuCATH is a glycine-rich cathelicidin containing 21 glycine residues.
source: Primary structural analysis indicated that PopuCATH is composed of 46 amino acid residues, including 41 polar residues and 5 non-polar residues, which is a glycine-rich cathelicidin (21 glycine residues) like those found in frog and fish (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents amino acid composition analysis showing 21 glycine residues out of 46 total residues.

claim: PopuCATH is composed of 46 amino acid residues.

evidence: The manuscript presents the complete amino acid sequence of the mature peptide.

claim: PopuCATH has net charges of +10.
source: PopuCATH has net charges of +10 and a theoretical isoelectric point of 12.60 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents calculated physicochemical properties based on the amino acid sequence.

claim: PopuCATH has a theoretical isoelectric point of 12.60.

claim: PopuCATH didn't show any antimicrobial activity against the tested bacteria at the concentration up to 200 µg/mL.
source: To our surprise, PopuCATH didn't show any antimicrobial activity against the tested bacteria (a total of 40 strains) at the concentration up to 200 µg/mL, including Gram-negative bacteria, Gram-positive bacteria, fungi, and aquatic pathogenic bacteria (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The manuscript presents MIC data for 40 bacterial strains showing no antimicrobial activity.

claim: 200 µg/mL of PopuCATH did not reduce the CFUs of E. coli, S. aureus, C. albicans, and A. hydrophila after incubation for 1, 2, 3, and 4 hr.
source: Similarly, in time-kill assays, 200 µg/mL of PopuCATH did not reduce the CFUs of E. coli, S. aureus, C. albicans, and A. hydrophila after incubation for 1, 2, 3, and 4 hr, respectively (Figure 2A).

claim: 200 µg/mL of PopuCATH did not alter bacterial metabolic activity during the exponential growth phase of E. coli, S. aureus, C. albicans, and A. hydrophila.

claim: 200 µg/mL of PopuCATH did not alter the surface morphology of E. coli and S. aureus.

claim: PopuCATH (10 mg/kg) treatment at 8 hr or 4 hr before bacterial inoculation significantly reduced the bacterial load in tree frogs.

evidence: The manuscript presents bacterial load data from tree frog infection experiments.

claim: PopuCATH (10 mg/kg) treatment at 4 hr after bacterial inoculation did not significantly reduce the bacterial load in tree frogs.

evidence: The manuscript presents bacterial load data from tree frog infection experiments.

claim: At concentration up to 200 μg/mL, PopuCATH didn't show any cytotoxicity to mouse peritoneal macrophages and human monocyte THP-1 cells.

claim: At concentration up to 200 μg/mL, PopuCATH didn't show any hemolytic activity to mouse erythrocytes and rabbit erythrocytes.
source: At concentration up to 200 μg/mL, PopuCATH didn't show any cytotoxicity to mouse peritoneal macrophages and humane monocyte THP-1 cells (Figure 3A), and didn't show any hemolytic activity to mouse erythrocytes and rabbit erythrocytes (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript presents hemolysis assay data showing no hemolytic activity.

claim: PopuCATH did not induce proliferation of lymphocytes isolated from mouse MLN and spleen at any dose tested up to 200 μg/mL.

claim: PopuCATH did not induce mast cell degranulation at any dose tested up to 200 mg/mL.

evidence: The manuscript presents mast cell degranulation assay data showing no hypersensitivity effect, with citation to previous work on LL-37.

claim: Human cathelicidin LL-37 markedly induced mast cell degranulation.

claim: PopuCATH didn't exhibit significant effect on complement activation at concentration up to 200 μg/mL.

claim: PopuCATH treatment did not cause pathological abnormality in kidney, liver, heart, and spleen at any dose tested up to 40 mg/kg.

claim: The levels of alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and creatinine in the sera of mice between PopuCATH- and PBS-treated groups showed no significant difference.

claim: The maximum tolerable dose of PopuCATH by intravenous delivery was between 75 and 100 mg/kg.

claim: The maximum tolerable dose of PopuCATH by intraperitoneal delivery was between 125 and 150 mg/kg.

evidence: The manuscript presents maximum tolerable dose determination data from mouse experiments.

claim: PopuCATH injection at –8 or –4 hr significantly reduced the bacterial loads in the abdominal cavity of mice post Gram-negative bacteria (E. coli, A. baumannii) and Gram-positive bacteria (S. aureus, methicillin-resistant S. aureus, MRSA) inoculation.

claim: PopuCATH injection at –8 or –4 hr significantly reduced the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines in mouse serum.

claim: E. coli or S. aureus inoculation markedly induced inflammatory damage in the lung.

claim: PopuCATH injection at –4 or –8 hr obviously rescued inflammatory damage in the lung induced by bacterial inoculation.

claim: An intraperitoneal injection of PopuCATH (10 mg/kg) significantly induced the recruitment of leukocytes in the peripheral blood of mice.
